intro: Marcelle Meyer plays Debussy’s drowned cathedral: distant bells rise into a great C-major organ, then sink beneath the water. One piano supplies the whole building.

sections.mNote: Open fifths rise above widely spaced bass notes

relations.label: The broad melody returns as an echo
relations.basis: Debussy recalls the broad chordal melody in the quieter, lower-register echo section. The matched excerpts lie within the first chordal statement and the echo marked near 268 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.908, sustained 12.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 141.5 s (cache/form/debussy-cathedrale-engloutie.txt, candidate 3; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Bells in the mist
cues.text: G and D sound across the piano, with a great space between them. Open fifths climb slowly through the middle. Debussy marks the opening Profondément calme, deeply calm, and places it in a gently ringing mist. The bass descends as the bells keep rising.
cues.evidence: Debussy, Préludes I, no. 10, bars 1–6; Piano Practical Editions, Centenary Edition (2018), p. 67. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/42/IMSLP881620-PMLP2394-Preludes_book_1_.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The drowned city of Ys
cues.text: In the Breton legend, the cathedral of Ys lies beneath the sea. On clear mornings it rises from the water; bells toll, priests chant and the organ sounds before the building sinks again. Debussy prints its name only after the last bar.
cues.evidence: The legend is summarised in the Centenary Edition, p. 66, and at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_cath%C3%A9drale_engloutie. The title follows bar 89 in the score.

cues.title: Out of the mist
cues.text: The bass slips down from C to B. Beneath the rising chords, the left hand starts rolling in triplets, and B major shines through. Debussy writes Peu à peu sortant de la brume: little by little, emerging from the mist.
cues.evidence: Score, bars 14–19, Centenary Edition, pp. 67–68: bass C–B, triplet accompaniment and Peu à peu sortant de la brume.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An organ without pipes
cues.text: The piano gathers around a G dominant seventh, then plants a low C beneath a procession of full chords. The melody moves inside them, doubled through both hands. Debussy asks for Sonore sans dureté — sonorous without harshness — even at fortissimo.
cues.evidence: Score, bars 22–41, Centenary Edition, pp. 68–69: G dominant-seventh preparation, low C, parallel chords and Sonore sans dureté at bar 28.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A chant in shadow
cues.text: The C-major chords fall quiet. An earlier chant returns in C♯ minor, low in the piano, above a held bass. Debussy asks for a little more movement and an expression that keeps growing; the small phrase climbs towards a second great chordal crest.
cues.evidence: Score, bars 42–61, Centenary Edition, pp. 70–71: C♯-minor recall of bars 7–13, Un peu moins lent and dans une expression allant grandissant.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The organ under water
cues.text: The broad C-major tune returns pianissimo, lower on the keyboard. Quavers rock beneath it like water moving around a submerged bell. Debussy calls the melody an echo of the phrase heard earlier, and marks the bass flottant et sourd — floating and muffled.
cues.evidence: Score, bars 72–83, Centenary Edition, pp. 71–72: C-major chordal return, Comme un écho de la phrase entendue précédemment, and flottant et sourd.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The last bells
cues.text: The rocking bass stops. Rising fifths recall the opening, now resting on C. The last chord holds a D among the notes of C major: one small note keeps ringing against the settled harmony.
cues.evidence: Score, bars 84–89, Centenary Edition, p. 72: Dans la sonorité du début, rising fifths, and final C-major chord with added D.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: C slips down to B
transitions.how: The rising fifths return over a low C. The bass then drops a semitone to B, and the left hand begins rolling triplets under the B-major chords. Debussy marks the passage as gradually emerging from the mist, while the right hand keeps the opening’s upward shape.
transitions.evidence: Score, bars 14–19, Centenary Edition, pp. 67–68: C–B bass, B-major passage and triplet accompaniment.

transitions.title: G prepares the organ’s low C
transitions.to: B · The organ in C major
transitions.how: The rising figures pass from B major through E♭ major to a G dominant seventh. The left-hand triplets stop. After a broad preparation, a low C supports the fortissimo melody in parallel chords, with both hands moving like an organist’s.
transitions.evidence: Score, bars 16–28, Centenary Edition, pp. 68–69: B major, E♭ major, G dominant seventh and the C-major chordal statement.

transitions.title: The chant returns in C♯ minor
transitions.from: B · The organ in C major
transitions.to: C · A chant in C♯ minor
transitions.how: The organ-like chords soften into widely spaced bell notes. C♯ minor then replaces C major, and the chant first heard near the opening returns low in the piano. The bass is held beneath it; Un peu moins lent starts the next ascent.
transitions.evidence: Score, bars 42–53, Centenary Edition, p. 70: bell-like withdrawal and C♯-minor chant from bar 47.

transitions.title: Seventh chords sink towards the echo
transitions.from: C · A chant in C♯ minor
transitions.how: The second crest subsides through parallel seventh chords. A low quaver figure begins to rock, and the earlier C-major melody returns above it, pianissimo. The tune now lies lower in the piano, explicitly marked as an echo.
transitions.evidence: Score, bars 61–75, Centenary Edition, p. 71: parallel seventh chords, oscillating bass and quiet C-major return.

transitions.title: The rocking bass stops
transitions.how: The quaver accompaniment stops on a low C. The piano returns to the opening’s rising fifths, marked Dans la sonorité du début. Slow bell chords remain, and the last C-major chord keeps D sounding inside it.
transitions.evidence: Score, bars 82–89, Centenary Edition, p. 72: end of the quavers, opening fifths and final added D.

composer.epithet: He trusted his ear over the rules — “pleasure is the law” — and made the piano, the flute and the orchestra sound new.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
Symbolist poetry · Mussorgsky · the Javanese gamelan · Couperin and Rameau
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, on 22 August 1862. His parents were not musicians. His father fought for the Paris Commune in 1871 and went to prison for it, and there he met Charles de Sivry, whose mother, Antoinette Mauté, taught the piano and said she had been a pupil of Chopin. She took the boy on. In 1872, aged ten, he entered the Paris Conservatoire.

His teachers could not make him out. Antoine Marmontel, his piano professor, found “a charming child, a truly artistic temperament” in January 1874; the harmony teacher Émile Durand reported in June 1879 that he was “very gifted in harmony, but hopelessly unfocused”. Years later, discussing chords at the piano with his old composition teacher Ernest Guiraud around 1890, he put his position plainly: “There is no theory. You merely have to listen. Pleasure is the law.”
